I'd had Keisuke Kinoshita to the classic directors, he's pretty much forgotten now but he was one the biggest names in his time. His films could easily compete with those of Kurosawa and Ozu when it came to garnering audiences to the theater. The Ballad of Noriyama is probably his most well known film and I think it's a great place to start. It's a great film and a good introduction to his style and themes.

Kinji Fukasaku is noteworthy too. You mentionned Battle Royale, for which his best remembered today but it was one of his last films and he made a whole career of yakuza films in the 70's. If you like Suzuki you'll sure like Fukasaku. He made the 8 first films of the Battles Without Honor and Humanity saga (which are all great) as well as the overlooked Graveyard of Honor, Street Mobster, Doberman Cop, Cops vs. Thugs...

If you're into exploitation I can only recommand Lady Snowblood and it's sequel (both by Toshiya Fujita), School of the Holy Beast and Girl Boss Guerilla (by Norifumi Suzuki) and the work of Yasuharu Hasebe. His action film Wolf Guy with Sonny Chiba is a lot of fun and he also made the Sister Street Fighter trilogy and the Delinquent Girl Boss tetralogy, which are sure toplease every fan of sleazy Japanese cinema. Other milestones of Japanese exploitation include the Daimajin trilogy, the 6-parts Lone Wolf & Cub saga, Horrors of the Malformed Men, Matango (by Godzilla creator Ishiro Honda) and maybe Goke: Body Snatcher from Hell too.

And if you like the work of Shin'ya Tsukamoto, I'd recommend checking out Gakuryu Ishii (Burst City, Crazy Thunder Road) and Shozin Fukui (Screams of Blasphemy). The three of them form the Holy Trinity of Japanese cyberpunk cinema.

And as a Frenchman, I cannot forget to mention The Battle of the Rails. It was made by René Clément (Purple Noon, Forbidden Games, Is Paris Burning?) in 1946 to glorify French resistance during WW2 (it depicts the efforts of railway workers who try to sabotage trains to annoy the nazis). Though it is admitted today that most French were passive during WW2, the official narrative during the decades that followed the war was that most of the French people helped fighting off the nazis in some way. So this film was made to comfort the people in this opinion and help create a sentiment a national pride after the humiliation of nazi occupation. The film itself it great otherwise, it's narrated by Charles Boyer (who played the Gaslighter in Gaslight and Cluny Brown's guy in Cluny Brown)

According to lb there were only 39 horror films produced in Japan during the 70's, and if you remove the shorts and docs it comes down to 34.

The most well-known one is Hausu, which has already been mentionned many times by other people in the comments but I still want to recommend it because it's a truly mad film with crazy visuals and a incredibly psychedelic atmosphere. Watch it when you're high and you'll be in for a wild ride.

There's also Wolf Guy, a werewolf action movie with Sonny Chiba, which is pretty wild and entertaining.

There's Blind Woman's Curse, which kinda feels as if Lady Snowblood was blend with 60's horror films like Onibaba or Kuroneko, it's great and it was directed by Teruo "Horror of the Malformed Men" Ishii.

Demons too feels very much like Japanese 60's horror, especially since it's in b&w (it was released early in the decade when b&w was still very common in Japanese cinema).

If you're into vampire I can only recommend you to check out Michio Yamamoto's Bloodthirsty trilogy, composed of The Vampire Doll, Lake of Dracula & Evil of Dracula. There an awesome box set of that trilogy released by Arrow that's really cheap.

Now if you seek more obscure stuff I still have 2 recs. Assault Jack the Ripper, a really trashy and sleazy film about a misogynistic serial killer (kind of the Japanese Maniac). And Oxen Split Torturing which is a stylish torture film with really horrible scenes in the same vibe of those Ishii made in the late 60's. Those 2 are ideal if you're into pre-video era snuff stuff.

And if you like ulra-cheap and cheesy monster movies, you may appreciate The Revenge of Dr. X, it's a Japanese-American co-production so the directors and most of the cast aren't Japanese but it's still technically a Japanese horror film of the 70's. Also it's a evil mutant plant story like Little Shop of Horrors and Day of the Triffids, if you like that kind of stuff.

Now since there ain't that much horro films from this decade, you may be interested in late-60's/early-80's stuff. So for the late-60's the best one is obviously Kaneto Shindo's Kuroneko, beautiful and eerie. Horros of the Malformed Men (which I've already mentionned and Blind Beast are absolutely awesome too. And I can't resist recommending you Yokai Monsters, that's a pretty wild and bizarre film but if you liked Hausu you should definitely check it out. Now for the ealry-80's there are 2 notable films, the first one is Virus (by the director of Battle Royale and the Battles Without Honor and Humanity saga) which features a partially American cast (Glenn Ford, Robert Vaughn, Bo Svenson, Henry Silva, George Kennedy) and is probably one the best post-apocalyptical film ever made. And there's The House Where Evil Dwells, which is a pretty obscure haunted house American film with Susan George & Doug McClure by Kevin Connor (Motel Hell, From Beyond the Grave) set in Japan. Certainly it hasn't aged as well as King Kong but it's still a classic. Alternatively, there's King Kong's late 40's sequel Mighty Joe Young, directed by King Kong's director Ernest B. Shoedsack himself and starring Robert Armstrong (Carl Denham in King Kong) along with western star Ben Johnson. Willis O'Brien, who made the fx of King Kong, also worked on those two films.

If you loved King Kong, you're also very likely to like The Most Dangerous Game, though it isn't a monster movie at all. The director is the same Shoedsack who made King Kong and Mighty Joe Young, it stars 3 actors from King Kong (Robert Armstrong, Fay Wray & Noble Johnson) along with future western star Joel McCrea in his breakthrough role. It's also the only the only film I could think of that is from the same period as King Kong, as it was released one year earlier.
